senses.gloss:
Mīrābāī
(A. D. 1547-1614)
------------------------------------------
One of the brightest jewels of the भक्ति Movement—a movement that raised, roused and united the common masses as well as the blue bloods through divine love—was मीराबाई.
She was born as the daughter of Ratan Singh at Kudki, a village in Rajasthan. When she was still three years old, she was tremendously attracted by the image of Giridhar (Lord कृष्ण) that a sādhu (a holy man) had brought. Her piteous pleadings ultimately forced the sādhu to leave the image with her.
When she was five, a मर्रिअगे party was passing by the road in front of her palatial होउसे. She innocently asked her मोथेर् who her bridegroom would be. Her मोथेर् smilingly replied that Giridhar was her bridegroom.
MīrābāīAnd, this statement stuck very deeply in her heart.
She lost her मोथेर् when she was just eight years old.
She was married to the prince Bhojrāj, the crown-prince of Mahārāṇa Saṅga, the king of Mewar with the capital at Chittore. At her husband’s होउसे she refused to bow down to their family deity दुर्गा since she would recognise and honour only her Giridhar! Thus started a series of frictions and troubles for her in the family.
When Bhojrāj died four years later Mīrā intensified her spiritual sādhanas after receiving initiation from Raidas, the famous saint of the day.
Soon after, Rāṇā Saṅga too passed away and his second son Vikramjit ascended the throne. Considering Mīrā’s ascetic way of life as also the congregational singing with devotees and mendicants as a slur on the royal family, the Rāṇā tried his best to harass her, and even kill her. But Giridhar was there always by her side to protect her even as he had protected प्रह्लाद, the child-devotee, ages ago.
Mīrā finally left Chittore and travelling all the way like a mendicant, through the various places of पिल्ग्रिमगे such as वृन्दाबन्, she finally settled down at द्वारका in Gujarat.
At वृन्दाबन् she is said to have gone to meet जीव Gosvāmi, a famous Vaiṣṇava saint. When he refused to meet her since she was a woman, she retorted that she thought in the world (and especially in वृन्दाबन्) there was only one man—that was Lord Kṛṣṇa—and all the others were women (prakṛti)! She was now surprised to find another man! This opened the inner eye of the Gosvāmi who begged her pardon.
Uday Singh, the new king of Mewar, being urged by the people to bring back Mīrā (whose banishment was thought to be the chief cause for the troubles of Mewar) sent a batch of holy persons with the chief priest (rājaguru) as the leader for the purpose. Mīrā did not agree but was merged in the image of the Lord in the temple.
Mīrā was the paragon of the madhura-भाव or bridal म्य्स्तिचिस्म्.
Mīrā’s songs are all composed in Brajbhāṣā, a dialect of Hindi, more common in Brajbhūmi (Mathurā-वृन्दाबन् area). About 500 songs are available now.
Most of the songs are on Śrī कृष्ण though a few are on राम and the efficacy of Rāmanāma. The theme is mostly pining for her Lord. Some of the songs however contain hints for sādhanā or spiritual practice also.
